title: Role-play lab: six bias conversations
objectives: Answer six bias conversations using empathy, goals and rules — never promises.
Use the module's scenario answers (Q21–Q25) as trainer-marked practice.
body_md:
In pairs. One person plays the client, one the distributor. The trainer scores on the points listed.

| # | Scenario | Bias | What a good response includes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Markets have fallen 15% in a month. A client with a 10-year goal calls to stop all SIPs. | Loss aversion | Empathy first; goal and horizon; SIP buys more units; reminder of their own plan; no promise of recovery. |
| 2 | A client wants to move everything into a small-cap fund that "everyone in the WhatsApp group" is buying. | Herd / FOMO | Checks allocation and risk profile; explains buying after a rally; suggests limiting it to a planned share, if any. |
| 3 | A client refuses to sell a long-underperforming fund until it "gets back to what I paid". | Anchoring, sunk cost | Separates purchase price from future prospects; compares with benchmark and alternatives; mentions tax and exit load. |
| 4 | A client has ₹20 lakh sitting in a savings account "until the market settles". | Inertia, regret aversion | Shows the cost of waiting; proposes an STP over 6–12 months; ties money to goals. |
| 5 | A client in IT has 70% of their wealth in their employer's shares. | Familiarity | Explains doubled risk (job and savings); proposes gradual diversification with tax planning. |
| 6 | Your manager tells you to pitch last year's top fund to every client this month. | Distributor's own bias | Raises suitability concerns; uses the checklist; recommends only where it fits the client. |

> **Investor takeaway:** Quiz scenarios Q21–Q25 (trainer-marked): a scenario answer earns its mark if it covers at least three model points and makes no promise of returns.
example: Role-play the fall: empathy first, goal and horizon, SIP buys more units, reminder of their own plan, no promise of recovery.
say: Empathy first; goal and horizon; no promise of recovery.
Use the suitability checklist for every recommendation.
never: Pressure a client to stay invested against their stated needs.
Use FOMO or fear in your own sales pitch.

check.q: Markets have fallen 15% in a month. A client with a 10-year goal calls to stop all SIPs. How do you respond?
o: Agree and stop all SIPs immediately

Acknowledge the feeling; reconnect to the goal and 10-year horizon; explain the SIP buys more units at lower prices; remind them of their signed plan; use history as context without promising recovery; record the call
Promise the market will recover next month
Switch everything to debt at once
check.why: Acknowledge the feeling; reconnect to the goal and 10-year horizon; explain that the SIP is buying more units at lower prices; remind them of their signed plan; use history as context without promising recovery; record the call.

check.q: A client wants to move everything into a small-cap fund “everyone in the WhatsApp group” is buying. How do you respond?
o: Name it gently as following the crowd; check fit with the target allocation and risk profile; explain popular often means it has already run up; if appropriate, limit it to a planned slice; never pitch using FOMO
check.why: Name it gently as following the crowd; check fit with the target allocation and risk profile; explain that popular often means it has already run up; if appropriate, limit it to a planned slice; never pitch using FOMO.

check.q: A client has ₹20 lakh in a savings account “until the market settles”. What do you suggest?
o: Show the cost of waiting (inflation, missed compounding); link the money to specific goals; propose an STP from a liquid or debt fund into equity over 6–12 months to reduce regret
Wait for a crash before investing anything
Put it all in a sectoral fund now
check.why: Show the cost of waiting (inflation, missed compounding); link the money to specific goals; propose an STP from a liquid or debt fund into equity over 6–12 months to reduce regret.
